H1.text: A glass of water. The air you breathe. A spoon of sugar stirred into tea.

H2.text: All three look smooth and even. But only one of them is a single pure substance.

H3.text: Diya fills her bottle at the college water cooler, and remembers a question.

H4.text: Is air a compound, like water? Or a mixture, like sweet tea?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will sort any substance into its right box.

P2.text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It comes in three states.

P3.text: A solid has a fixed shape and volume. Its particles sit close and only shake in place.

P4.text: A liquid has a fixed volume, but takes the shape of its container. Its particles slide past each other.

P5.text: A gas has neither. Its particles fly apart and fill any space they get.

P6.text: Change the temperature or the pressure, and one state turns into another. Ice melts into water, and water boils into vapour.

U1.text: Now let's sort matter into boxes. Every sample is either a mixture or a pure substance.

U2.text: A mixture holds two or more substances, in any ratio.

U3.text: If it is the same all through, like sugar in water, it is homogeneous. Homo means same.

U4.text: If it is not the same everywhere, like salt mixed with sugar, it is heterogeneous.

U5.text: A pure substance has only one kind of particle. An element has only one kind of atom, like copper or oxygen.

U6.text: A compound has atoms of different elements, joined in a fixed ratio, like water or carbon dioxide.

S1.text: Let's look inside air on our molecule bench.

S2.text: Dry air is about seventy eight percent nitrogen and twenty one percent oxygen. The rest is mostly argon, with a little carbon dioxide.

S3.text: Different molecules, just moving around together. No bonds hold them to each other.

S4.text: Now look at water. Every particle is the same. Two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

S5.text: Watch how water is made. Hydrogen and oxygen molecules break apart, and their electrons pair up in new bonds.

S6.text: The new substance is nothing like its parts. Hydrogen burns with a pop. Oxygen helps things burn. But water puts out fire.

B1.text: On the counter: air has many kinds of particles, in a ratio that can change. Water has one kind, in a fixed ratio.

B2.text: Pause and think. So is air a compound or a mixture?

B3.text: A mixture! Its gases are not bonded, the ratio can change, and each gas keeps its own properties.

D1.text: Here is how to sort any sample, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Does it have only one kind of particle? If not, it is a mixture.

D3.text: Step two. Is the mixture the same all through? Then it is homogeneous. If not, heterogeneous.

D4.text: Step three. A pure substance with just one kind of atom? Then it is an element.

D5.text: Step four. Different atoms, joined in a fixed ratio? Then it is a compound.

T1.text: Remember this. A mixture keeps its parts. A compound makes something new.

W2.text: Sort these six samples. Air, water, copper wire, sugar solution, salt with sugar, and oxygen gas.

W3.text: Copper wire holds only copper atoms. Element.

W4.text: Oxygen gas is O two. Both atoms are oxygen, so it is also an element.

W5.text: Water holds hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio. Compound.

W6.text: Air and sugar solution are the same all through. Homogeneous mixtures.

W7.text: Salt with sugar has separate grains. A heterogeneous mixture.

C1.text: A mixture can be split by physical methods. Nothing new is made.

C2.text: Hand picking lifts out large pieces, like stones from rice. Filtration holds back solids, like tea leaves in a strainer.

C3.text: Crystallisation grows pure crystals out of a solution. Distillation boils a liquid and collects its vapour.

C4.text: A compound cannot be split this way. Its atoms are bonded, so it needs a chemical method, like an electric current that splits water.

X2.text: Some students call oxygen gas a compound, because O two has two atoms.

X3.text: But both atoms are oxygen. One kind of atom means an element. Hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen gases are all elements.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As short questions to classify a sample, or true or false statements.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which set lists a homogeneous mixture, a compound and an element, in that order? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Air, water, oxygen.

A2.text: Air is a homogeneous mixture. Water is a compound. Oxygen gas has one kind of atom, so it is an element.

A3.text: B fails: salt with sugar is heterogeneous.

A4.text: C puts the element before the compound. D calls ozone a compound, but ozone, O three, is still an element.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is air a mixture and not a compound?

Y3.text: Two. Is nitrogen gas, N two, an element or a compound?

Y4.text: Three. How would you separate sand from water?
